## The findings

One finding — `crime_00024` — covers both declarations in `src/api/state.ts`. Verbatim evidence:

> - `"plural name, singular type: \`users: User\` @L24"`
> - `"singular name, array type: \`invoice: Invoice[]\` @L27"`
> - `"v1 detector — type aliases and generic types are silently skipped"`

Its `fix_shape` is `"make the name agree with the type — \`users\` for array, \`user\` for scalar"`, and the suggested action is:

> `"Rename the variable to match the type's shape, or change the type to match the name. If the project intentionally diverges, add the name to \`detectors.options.singular_plural_type_mismatch.allowedNames\`."`

The scan reports the name/type disagreement but not the third witness that breaks the tie — the initializer. Both declarations have one, and in both cases it sides with the type:

```ts
24  export const users: User = { id: "u_1", email: "a@b.c" };
27  export const invoice: Invoice[] = [];
```

## L24 — `users: User`

**Recommendation: (a) rename. The type carries the intended meaning.**

The initializer is a single object literal, not a collection. If you took option (b) and widened the type to `User[]`, the annotation would stop type-checking against the value — you'd have to rewrite the initializer to `[{ id: "u_1", … }]`, which changes what the module actually exports. Option (b) is a behaviour change wearing a naming fix's clothes; option (a) is a pure identifier change. When the value and the type agree and only the name dissents, the name is the outvoted party.

Caveat the scan can't see: `user: User` already exists at L33 as a negative control, so the obvious rename collides inside the same module. In this fixture, the plural is a deliberate demo of the miswording; in real code you'd resolve the collision by merging the two declarations or by qualifying the name to say which user it is (`currentUser`, `seedUser`) rather than reaching for a plural you don't have data for.

## L27 — `invoice: Invoice[]`

**Recommendation: (a) rename. The type carries the intended meaning.**

Same reasoning, one degree stronger. The initializer is `[]` — an empty array is unambiguously a collection, and an empty *scalar* has no equivalent. Narrowing the type to `Invoice` under option (b) would leave you with no legal initializer at all short of inventing a fake invoice or reaching for `null`/`undefined` and changing the exported type to `Invoice | undefined`. The array shape is load-bearing; `invoice` is just a typo-level singular.

Same collision caveat: `invoices: Invoice[]` already exists at L34.

## Two things worth knowing before you act

**The detector under-reports this file.** Its own evidence says `"v1 detector — type aliases and generic types are silently skipped"`. Any `const x: SomeAlias` or `const y: Array<Invoice>` in this file was never examined, so the two hits are a floor, not a census. `Array<Invoice>` in particular would be exactly this bug and would go unseen.

**If you're tempted by option (b), check the contract findings first.** `crime_00032` and `crime_00033` both fire on this file: this module's `User` (2 fields, L4) and `Invoice` (2 fields, L9) each disagree with a same-named interface in `src/billing.ts` (5 and 11 fields). Per `crime_00033`, `Invoice` here is missing `createdAt`, `currency`, `discountCents`, `subtotalCents`, `taxCents`, and `userId`. Reshaping these types to fix a naming complaint would deepen a `high`-severity split-brain to settle a `low`-severity one — another reason the rename is the right side to move.

Both fixes are `"effort": "quick"` and carry `"risk": "low"`. Nothing in the repo imports `src/api/state.ts` — I grepped, there are no call sites — so the renames are contained to this file, and the only real constraint is the same-module collision with the L33/L34 controls.
